migrationNotes: Spine: one noisy parents' meeting about Jo's canteen idea supplies each slip in turn, a reply aimed at the person, then at a view nobody held, then a shifting word, a circle and a forced choice, and the lesson ends by turning the test on yourself: rebuild an argument at its strongest before you answer it.

lesson.title: Fallacies and charity

steps.headline: Fallacies, starting with attacks on the person

lead.text: The neighbour's remark is an example of a fallacy: a pattern of reasoning that looks convincing and fails. Fallacies are worth learning because they come back. The same few slips turn up in school meetings and in parliament alike, and once you can name one you can spot it each time it returns.

This one has a Latin name, ad hominem, which means “to the person”. It dismisses an argument by pointing at something about the person who makes it, such as her diet or her job. Those facts can matter when you are deciding whether to trust what someone reports. They can't settle whether the reasons she gives are good. Jo's case can be weighed against the price of greens and the health of the children, whatever she eats at home.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets out the neighbour's reply as an argument. To make it work you have to supply an unstated premise, as in the first lesson: that nothing a vegetarian says about school meals deserves attention. Written out, it is plainly too strong to accept. A good test for this slip is to imagine someone else, a meat-eater, making the same suggestion. The reply no longer applies, which shows it was never about the suggestion.

model.passage: Jo's a vegetarian, so ignore her.

premises.text: Nothing a vegetarian says about school meals deserves attention.

model.passage: Ignore her review of the phone, since she works in the shop.

premises.text: She works in the phone shop.
Nothing a shop worker says about a phone deserves attention.

conclusion.text: Her review of the phone can be ignored.

lead.text: Compare what Dr Okafor argued with what the councillor answered. Then give the pattern its name.

Suppose the meeting returns to Jo's idea and she makes it specific: one meat-free day a week in the canteen. A parent answers, “So Jo wants to stop our children eating meat.” That reply answers a different proposal from the one Jo made. She suggested one day a week, and the parent has answered a ban.

Swapping someone's position for a weaker or more extreme one and then defeating that is called a straw man, after a man made of straw, who is easy to knock over. The reply may even be a good one against the ban. It simply doesn't touch Jo's view, so her proposal is left standing. The figure follows the arrow from the parent's reply, once to the wrong target and once, in the second view, to the right one.

diagram.alt: Two columns. On the left is what Jo said, one meat-free day a week. A straw-man reply points to a different claim on the right, a ban on children eating meat, and never reaches Jo's proposal. A fair reply points at her proposal.
diagram.caption: Follow the arrow from the reply. A straw man lands on a claim nobody made. A fair reply lands on the claim that was made. Use the buttons to compare them.

afterFigure.text: The cure is a habit. Before you answer anyone, restate their view in words they would accept, and check that what you are about to attack is that view. The same habit matters again at the end of this lesson.

lead.text: Compare Ana's proposal with the one Ben goes on to criticise. Then name what he has done.

Some slips hide inside a single word. Here is a small case: “Nothing is better than a day at the beach. A cold, wet Monday is better than nothing. So a cold, wet Monday is better than a day at the beach.” Each premise is acceptable on its own, and the conclusion is plainly wrong.

The trouble is the word “nothing”. In the first premise it means that no activity beats a day at the beach. In the second it means the absence of anything at all. The argument only seems to work because the same word appears twice. Using a word in two senses within one argument is called equivocation. Words with two ordinary meanings, such as “bank” and “fine”, are the usual culprits. The figure shows where the word sits in each premise.

diagram.alt: A ranking from worse to better. In the first premise the word nothing marks an empty place above a day at the beach, meaning no activity is better. In the second premise nothing is an empty day ranked below a cold, wet Monday.
diagram.caption: The word “nothing” in each premise. Use the buttons to compare the two meanings.

lead.text: Check whether the key word keeps one meaning throughout this argument.

steps.headline: Going in circles, and false choices

lead.text: Two more slips concern the support itself. The first is begging the question: a premise that already assumes the conclusion. Take “Parking in the town centre should be free, because it ought not to cost anything to park there.” The reason is the conclusion in other words, so nothing has been added. The circle can be wider and pass through several claims, but it always returns to its starting point.

The second is the false dilemma, which offers two options as if they were the only ones. Back at the meeting someone says, “Either the canteen serves chips every day or the children go hungry.” It sounds forceful because the second option is unthinkable, but the speaker has not shown that there is no third. The question to ask of any either-or is what else is possible. The figure draws each slip in turn.

afterFigure.text: Both slips can be caught by looking at the support. For a circle, trace where the reason comes from and see whether it leads back to the claim. For a dilemma, count the options offered and then count the options that exist.

diagram.alt: Two drawings. In the first, a conclusion about free parking and the reason offered for it say the same thing, so the support loops back to the claim. In the second, an either-or offers two doors, chips every day or hungry children, and leaves out a third door of other options.
diagram.caption: Two ways support can fail. Use the buttons to see a circle, and then an either-or with a missing option.

The third is the one the either-or leaves out.</text><text x="24" y="358" class="t-small t-muted">Count the options offered, then count the options that exist.</text></svg>

lead.text: Trace where the support for the claim comes from. Then choose what is wrong with this piece of reasoning.

Every slip so far makes a reply easier than it should be, and the straw man is the clearest case: it picks the weakest version of a view and calls the job done. The remedy has a name, the principle of charity. Before you criticise an argument, rebuild it in the strongest form its author could reasonably accept, and answer that.

Charity often means supplying a premise, as you did in the first lesson. Return to Jo, who said, “Children aren't eating enough vegetables, so the canteen should serve more.” The step between the two halves is unstated. A weak reading fills it with “Schools should force children to eat vegetables”, which is easy to attack and which Jo never said. A charitable reading fills it with something she would accept, such as “A school canteen should make it easier for children to eat what they are short of”. The figure shows both readings.

afterFigure.text: The charitable reading is the better one to answer, and the reason is practical as well as polite. If you can beat the strongest version, your reply also covers the weaker ones, and if you can't, you have learned something about the argument. You may still reject the argument at the end. If you do, you will have rejected something its author actually holds.

model.passage: Children aren't eating enough vegetables, so the canteen should serve more.

premises.text: Children at the school aren't eating enough vegetables.
A school canteen should make it easier for children to eat what they are short of.

conclusion.text: The canteen should serve more vegetables.

model.passage: Children aren't eating enough vegetables, so the canteen should serve more.

premises.text: Children at the school aren't eating enough vegetables.
Schools should force children to eat vegetables.

conclusion.text: The canteen should serve more vegetables.

lead.text: Charity starts with stating the other person's view fairly. Look at what happens when that step is skipped.
Now use charity on a new argument. Choose the added premise that a thoughtful speaker would accept and that makes the step from reason to conclusion work.

model.passage: Smoking causes cancer, so you shouldn't smoke.

premises.text: You should avoid what greatly raises your risk of a serious disease.
Smoking greatly raises the risk of lung cancer.

model.passage: Dogs should be kept on leads in the park, since they chase the ducks.

premises.text: Dogs in the park chase the ducks.
Animals that harass wildlife should be restrained.

conclusion.text: Dogs should be kept on leads in the park.

lesson.orientation: Name common informal fallacies and reconstruct an opponent's argument in its most plausible form.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: At a parents' meeting, Jo says the school canteen should serve more vegetables. Her neighbour leans over and murmurs, “Jo's a vegetarian, so ignore her.” A few people smile, and the meeting moves on to the car park.

Nothing in the neighbour's reply needs to be false, because Jo may well be a vegetarian. It still goes wrong. It sounds like a reason, with a “so” in the middle, but it says nothing about whether the canteen should serve more vegetables. Last lesson tested whether premises hold up a conclusion. Here the premise doesn't touch the matter at all, and that is only one of several ways in which reasoning can mislead.

This lesson names the commonest of these slips so you can spot them in other people's reasoning and in your own. It ends with the other half of the skill, which is answering someone's argument at its strongest instead of its weakest.

intro.promise: By the end you'll name common slips in reasoning and rebuild an opponent's argument in its strongest form before you reply.

recap.keyIdea: Name the slip, then answer the best version. Replies go wrong by targeting the person, a different view, a shifting word, a circle or a false choice, and charity means rebuilding the argument fairly before you reply.

blocks.text: You started with a neighbour's brush-off at a parents' meeting and followed the meeting through four more slips: a reply aimed at a view nobody held, a word that changed meaning, a circular reason and a forced choice. You ended by rebuilding Jo's argument at its strongest and choosing the fairest premise for a new one.

recap.nextHook: Arguments are not only about logic. The next lesson asks what it takes for a belief to count as knowledge.

questions.prompt: Dr Okafor argues that a bridge design is unsafe. A councillor replies: 'She once lost a contract to that firm, so we can ignore her.' Name the fallacy.
hints: Does the reply engage with the reasons about the bridge, or with something else?
The fallacy has a Latin name meaning 'to the person'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ad hominem: the reply targets the arguer's history instead of her calculations.

questions.onCorrect: Ad hominem: the reply targets the arguer's history instead of her calculations.

misconceptions.feedback: The reply does not misstate her view. Look at what it attacks instead.

questions.prompt: Ana: 'Speed limits beside schools should drop to 20 mph.' Ben: 'Ana wants every car in the country crawling along at 20, which would wreck the economy.' Name Ben's fallacy.
hints: Compare Ana's actual proposal with the one Ben criticises.
The fallacy is named after a figure that is easy to knock down.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A straw man: Ben attacks a national limit that Ana never proposed.

questions.onCorrect: A straw man: Ben attacks a national limit that Ana never proposed.

misconceptions.feedback: Ben does not attack Ana herself. Compare her proposal with the one he criticises.

questions.prompt: 'A feather is light. Whatever is light is not dark. So a feather is not dark.' Name the fallacy.
hints: Ask whether 'light' means the same thing in both premises.
The fallacy's name comes from Latin for 'equal voice': one word, two senses.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equivocation: 'light' means 'not heavy' in one premise and 'pale' in the other.

questions.onCorrect: Equivocation: “light” shifts from “not heavy” to “pale” between the premises.

misconceptions.feedback: The slip is inside the words. Check whether “light” keeps one meaning throughout.

questions.prompt: Someone says: 'Smoking causes cancer, so you shouldn't smoke.' Which added premise gives the most charitable reconstruction?
hints: Choose the premise that is believable and still connects the reason to the conclusion.

acceptedIdeas: You should avoid what greatly raises your risk of a serious disease
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is plausible and makes the argument valid. The other two are false or much stronger than the speaker needs.

choices.label: You should avoid what greatly raises your risk of a serious disease
Anything that causes something bad should be banned

questions.onCorrect: The believable premise makes the argument valid and worth answering. Charity picks the strongest version.

misconceptions.feedback: That premise is false, so it makes the argument easy to dismiss. Charity looks for one a thoughtful speaker would accept.
That is much stronger than the speaker needs. Charity does not add more than the argument requires.

questions.prompt: 'This newspaper never prints falsehoods. We know this because its front page says so, and that statement must be true, since the paper never prints falsehoods.' Name the fallacy.
hints: Trace where the support for 'never prints falsehoods' comes from.
The argument travels in a circle back to its starting claim.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Begging the question: the conclusion is used to support the premise offered for it.

questions.onCorrect: Begging the question: the claim is used to support the very statement offered for it.

misconceptions.feedback: The passage offers no choice between options. Trace where its support for the claim comes from.

questions.prompt: 'Either we close the library or the council goes bankrupt.' The council in fact has several other ways to save money. Name the fallacy.
hints: Count the options the speaker offers, then the options that really exist.
The fallacy is named after a forced choice between two horns.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A false dilemma: two options are presented as the only ones when others exist.

questions.onCorrect: A false dilemma: two options are presented as the only ones when others exist.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing is assumed in a premise here. Count the options offered against those that exist.

questions.prompt: Is the neighbour's reply a reason about the canteen at all? Answer yes or no.
hints: What does the reply say about vegetables on the menu?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. It says something about Jo, not about whether the canteen should serve more vegetables.

questions.onCorrect: The reply is about Jo, not the canteen. A good reply to an argument speaks to its reasons.

misconceptions.feedback: The reply is about Jo. Ask what it would say if someone else made the same suggestion.

questions.prompt: “You can trust the report, because the report says it is trustworthy.” What is wrong with this reasoning?
hints: Compare the claim with the reason given for it.

acceptedIdeas: The conclusion is assumed in the reason offered.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The conclusion is assumed in the reason offered.

choices.label: The conclusion is assumed in the reason offered.

questions.onCorrect: The reason just repeats the claim. An argument that assumes its conclusion adds no support.

misconceptions.feedback: No options are being offered here. Look at how the reason relates to the claim.
Nobody is attacked. Compare the claim with the reason given for it.

questions.prompt: Sam says, “We should add a bike lane on Mill Road.” Kit replies, “Sam wants to ban cars from the town.” Why does Kit's reply leave Sam's proposal untouched?
hints: Compare what Sam proposed with what Kit criticises.

acceptedIdeas: It attacks a different, more extreme position.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It attacks a different, more extreme position.

choices.label: It attacks a different, more extreme position.
It is spoken in a rude tone.
It gives no reasons at all.

questions.onCorrect: Kit's criticism may be good, but it aims at a position Sam never took.

misconceptions.feedback: Tone is not the fault. Compare what Sam proposed with what Kit criticises.
Kit does give a reason. The reason is aimed at the wrong target.

questions.prompt: Lena argues for longer library hours. Rob replies: “Lena wants the library open all night, every night, which would bankrupt us.” Name Rob's fallacy.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A straw man: Rob attacks an extreme version of Lena's proposal.

questions.onCorrect: Rob swaps in a more extreme view and refutes that. The restated proposal is what to answer.

misconceptions.feedback: Rob does not attack Lena herself. Compare her proposal with the one he criticises.

citations.claim: A fallacy is a pattern of reasoning that looks convincing but fails; rejecting an argument because of who offers it is the ad hominem fallacy.
